findings.source_passage: Adverse winds are holding mad Christmas in him, boys. It's the first foul wind I ever knew to blow from astern; but look, did ever whale yaw so before? it must be, he's lost his tiller.
findings.source_locator: Stubb's speech after 'Who's got some paregoric?'
findings.why_it_matters: This is the comic heart of Stubb's characterization in this chapter — grotesque, inventive, tonally distinct. The draft keeps only 'did ever whale yaw so before?' and erases the 'mad Christmas' and 'lost his tiller' lines entirely, collapsing a voice-establishing comic riff to a single question.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore Stubb's full speech: 'Adverse winds are holding mad Christmas in him, boys. It's the first foul wind I ever knew to blow from astern; but look, did ever whale yaw so before? it must be, he's lost his tiller.' These lines are irreplaceable voice material.

findings.source_passage: As an overladen Indiaman bearing down the Hindostan coast with a deck load of frightened horses, careens, buries, rolls, and wallows on her way; so did this old whale heave his aged bulk
findings.source_locator: Paragraph describing the old bull's motion, after Stubb's paregoric speech
findings.why_it_matters: This Indiaman simile is a prosodically distinctive, rhetorically elaborate set-piece that carries Melville's signature analogical style; it also anchors the reader's visual understanding of the bull's pathetic motion. Its total absence flattens a key descriptive passage.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the simile in at least compressed form: 'As an overladen Indiaman bearing down the Hindostan coast with a deck load of frightened horses, careens, buries, rolls, and wallows on her way; so did this old whale heave his aged bulk, and now and then partly turning over on his cumbrous rib-ends, expose the cause of his devious wake in the unnatural stump of his starboard fin.'

findings.source_passage: he mocks and dares me with the very poor-box I filled for him not five minutes ago!—then in his old intense whisper—Give way, greyhounds! Dog to it!
findings.source_locator: Starbuck's speech after Derick shakes the lamp-feeder
findings.why_it_matters: The 'poor-box' image is a distinctive, memorable figure that encapsulates Starbuck's moral sensibility and wounded dignity — a quotable line with interpretive weight about charity and rivalry. The draft cuts it entirely, preserving only the whisper 'Give way, greyhounds!' without its framing.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore: '"The ungracious and ungrateful dog!" cried Starbuck; "he mocks and dares me with the very poor-box I filled for him not five minutes ago!"—then in his old intense whisper—"Give way, greyhounds! Dog to it!"'

findings.source_passage: Is this the creature of whom it was once so triumphantly said—'Canst thou fill his skin with barbed irons?'… Oh! that unfulfilments should follow the prophets.
findings.source_locator: Central meditation after 'To three bits of board'
findings.why_it_matters: The full Job quotation with its ironic framing ('Is this the creature?') and the devastatingly compressed philosophical outcry ('Oh! that unfulfilments should follow the prophets') is interpretively critical — it is the chapter's thematic pivot on power and scripture. The draft reduces the passage to a bare quotation fragment without the framing sentences that give it meaning.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the complete framing: 'Is this the creature of whom it was once so triumphantly said—"Canst thou fill his skin with barbed irons? or his head with fish-spears?… he laugheth at the shaking of a spear!" This the creature? this he? Oh! that unfulfilments should follow the prophets.' The rhetorical structure must be preserved.

findings.source_passage: This puts me in mind of fastening to an elephant in a tilbury on a plain—makes the wheel-spokes fly, boys, when you fasten to him that way… this is the way a fellow feels when he's going to Davy Jones—all a rush down an endless inclined plane!
findings.source_locator: Stubb's speech after Derick is spilled, mid-speech
findings.why_it_matters: These lines are the rhetorical peak of Stubb's post-strike exuberance and exemplify Melville's comic grotesque at full register. The draft keeps the frame lines ('Every keel a sunbeam,' 'tin kettles,' 'everlasting mail') but drops the most inventive and voice-rich similes in the middle.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore at minimum: 'This puts me in mind of fastening to an elephant in a tilbury on a plain' and 'this is the way a fellow feels when he's going to Davy Jones—all a rush down an endless inclined plane!' between the surrounding kept lines.

findings.source_passage: as by magnetic wires, the life and death throbs of the whale, so that every oarsman felt them in his seat
findings.source_locator: Starbuck's 'Stand by, men; he stirs' passage
findings.why_it_matters: The phrase 'magnetic wires' is a characteristically Melvillean anachronistic precision that lodges in the reader's sensory imagination; 'as by wires' in the draft erases the 'magnetic' quality that makes the image distinctive.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore 'as by magnetic wires' in place of the draft's plain 'as by wires.'

findings.source_passage: with half-stifled melancholy gurglings the spray-column lowers and lowers to the ground—so the last long dying spout of the whale
findings.source_locator: Final description of the whale's death, the dying spout simile
findings.why_it_matters: The draft converts this into a truncated quotation fragment ('"As when by unseen hands…"') and omits 'half-stifled melancholy gurglings' — the sonic and emotional crux of the simile. The phrase is among the most elegiac in the chapter.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the full simile unquoted and untruncated, including 'with half-stifled melancholy gurglings the spray-column lowers and lowers to the ground.'

findings.source_passage: There she slides, now! Hurrah for the white-ash breeze! Down with the Yarman! Sail over him!
findings.source_locator: Paragraph describing the three mates' chivalrous advance, 'in that fine, loose, chivalrous attitude'
findings.why_it_matters: The mates' rally cry and the 'fine, loose, chivalrous attitude of the headsman' framing are both absent; this passage establishes the heroic-mock-epic register of the chase and the cry itself is a recognizable voice marker.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the 'chivalrous attitude' paragraph and the rallying cry: 'Hurrah for the white-ash breeze! Down with the Yarman! Sail over him!'

summary: The draft has multiple high-severity losses — Stubb's 'mad Christmas' speech, the Indiaman simile, Starbuck's 'poor-box' line, and the full Job-quotation interpretive frame — plus several medium-severity voice flattenings, collectively erasing the chapter's comic grotesque register and its central theological pivot.
